Why Your Gradebook Grade Changes When Work Is Ungraded

Understand current versus total grades, ungraded assignments and recorded zeros before using a gradebook percentage to plan your final.

By GradeTargetCalc · Published 2 November 2026 · 5 min read

In this guide
A different displayed grade does not always mean a new scoreFollow one record through two denominatorsSeparate ungraded, missing, excused and awarded-zero workRead your platform’s explanation, then the syllabusChoose the correct input for a final-exam calculationReconcile the display with a small worksheetAsk a precise question when totals still disagreeFAQsSources
01

A different displayed grade does not always mean a new score

You open your course page and see 86%. After changing a display option, the total becomes 51.6%, even though none of your marked assignments changed. Before assuming a grading mistake, check what each total includes. One number may summarize completed work; the other may spread those same earned contributions across the whole planned course.

The useful question is not which number looks more reassuring. Ask which record, weighting and reporting period each number represents. A current-grade percentage can be perfectly accurate for completed work while being unsuitable as a forecast of your final outcome.

02

Follow one record through two denominators

Imagine that completed assessments represent 60% of a course and average 86%. Their contribution is 86 × 0.60 = 51.6 course percentage points. The other 40% has not been assessed. A completed-work view divides the earned contribution by the completed fraction: 51.6 ÷ 0.60 = 86%.

A whole-course view that temporarily counts unfinished work as zero reports 51.6%. That does not mean the earlier 86% was erased. The same contribution is being interpreted against a different denominator. If the remaining work later averages 80%, it supplies another 32 points and the completed course becomes 83.6%.

03

Separate ungraded, missing, excused and awarded-zero work

A blank mark is a status requiring explanation, not a mathematical instruction. It might mean that feedback is pending, work is due later, a submission has not been recorded or an assessment is excluded. A recorded zero, by contrast, may be an actual awarded mark that belongs in the calculation.

Do not remove a genuine zero simply because excluding it raises your average. Equally, do not turn an unmarked future assessment into an awarded zero without checking the course policy. An excused assessment may require removing its possible points or redistributing weights, which changes the model again.

04

Read your platform’s explanation, then the syllabus

Canvas documents separate current and total grade views. Its student guidance explains that the current view uses graded work, while the total view also considers ungraded assignments. The exact options available can depend on the course configuration.

Treat that documentation as an explanation of a platform feature, not proof of your instructor’s intended reporting rule. Other systems may use different labels. Look for an inclusion checkbox, an assignment-status legend and a category-weight breakdown, then compare them with the syllabus rather than guessing from a large percentage at the top.

05

Choose the correct input for a final-exam calculation

A standalone final-grade calculation needs the normalized grade for all work other than that final. In the example, 86 is the relevant current average if the unfinished 40% consists entirely of the final. Entering 51.6 as the current grade would apply the completed-work fraction a second time.

If several assignments remain, a final-only model is incomplete. Use the earned 51.6 course points with the completed 60% weight in a remaining-work calculation. Also verify whether the final is a separate category or is added inside an existing test category, because those arrangements have different effective weights.

06

Reconcile the display with a small worksheet

Write down the information needed to reproduce the record before contacting your course team. A short worksheet often exposes a category mismatch or an accidentally included future zero faster than comparing two unexplained totals.

  • Record the reporting period, grading mode and date of the displayed total.
  • List awarded marks separately from pending, missing and excused items.
  • Confirm whether category percentages or pooled points determine the grade.
  • Rebuild one category and compare it with the gradebook breakdown.
  • Keep hypothetical what-if scores separate from actual awarded scores.
07

Ask a precise question when totals still disagree

If the difference remains, describe the specific inclusion rule you cannot reconcile. For example: “My graded quiz points total 43 out of 50, but the category shows 71.67%. Does it include an ungraded ten-point quiz?” This gives the instructor a reproducible issue rather than a request to choose the higher total.

A calculator cannot access hidden marks, alter a register or decide whether a late-work policy should apply. Use it to identify the source of the difference and to make planning assumptions explicit. Once the course team confirms the record, update your estimate using that clarified information.

Quick answers

Frequently asked questions

Is an ungraded assignment always a zero?

No. Its treatment depends on the assignment status, platform setting and course policy. A recorded awarded zero is different from a score that has not yet been entered.

Can switching a grade display change my official mark?

A display option changes what you see under its calculation assumptions. It does not by itself award marks or change the instructor’s recorded assessment results.

Which current grade should I use for a final target?

Use the normalized percentage for all non-final work, excluding the final itself. First confirm that no other unfinished work or category rule makes that standalone model incomplete.
